editorial:
Produced by National Film Corporation of America and distributed by First National Pictures, Tarzan of the Apes opened January 27, 1918 at the Broadway Theatre in New York â€” the first Tarzan film ever made. Director Scott Sidney cast Elmo Lincoln as adult Tarzan and Gordon Griffith as the boy, adapting Edgar Rice Burroughs' 1912 novel only six years after its magazine debut. The film was a landmark commercial hit, reportedly the first American feature to gross $1 million in domestic rentals, launching a franchise that has never stopped. The print survives, though the commonly circulating cut runs about 61 minutes against an original length exceeding 100 minutes.

For creators the film print is a fully free resource, with one concrete trap. Published in 1918, every US copyright term has elapsed by decades; the underlying Burroughs novel (first published 1912) is equally clear. The trap is trademark: Edgar Rice Burroughs, Inc.â€”the company Burroughs himself founded to control the franchiseâ€”holds active, aggressively enforced trademark rights in the Tarzan name and character. Distributing or exhibiting the film requires no copyright license whatsoever. Attaching the Tarzan brand to commercial products, merchandise, or a titled project requires a separate trademark clearance from ERB Inc., and the company is known to pursue infringers regardless of the film's public-domain status.
faq: Is the 1918 Tarzan of the Apes film in the public domain?

Yes, unambiguously. The film was released in the United States on January 27, 1918. The original 28-year US copyright term expired in 1946, and even if the copyright was renewed the second term would have expired no later than 1974. All works published in the US in 1930 or earlier are now in the public domain by term expiry â€” no renewal research is needed to confirm PD status for this film.
Can I use the Tarzan name and character in a commercial project based on this film?

Exhibiting or distributing the film itself is free. However, Edgar Rice Burroughs, Inc. holds active trademark rights over the 'Tarzan' name and character that survive the film's copyright expiry. Any commercial use of the Tarzan brand â€” titles, merchandise, sequels, branded content â€” requires a trademark license from ERB Inc. independent of the film's copyright status.
